notes: Community pack, roadmap Phase 1 candidate #1. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: The kitchen and the tools in it

themes.theme: A kitchen you can find things in
themes.description: Stations, storage and why every working kitchen puts the knife, the board and the bin within one step of each other.
themes.transfer_check: Reorganise one real kitchen work area so a named dish can be made without crossing the room, and show the before and after.

themes.theme: The knife and the hand that holds it
themes.description: Grip, claw, board stability and the three cuts that cover most of cooking.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the claw grip and produce even slices, dice and rough chop from real vegetables.

themes.theme: Heat: what pans and ovens actually do
themes.description: Conduction, radiant heat and preheating — why the pan matters more than the recipe line that names it.
themes.transfer_check: Cook the same ingredient in a cold-start and a preheated pan and explain the difference you can see and taste.

themes.theme: Fire, burns and the kitchen that bites
themes.description: Pan fires, steam, hot sugar and the responses that must be automatic before they are needed.
themes.transfer_check: Walk a real kitchen and state, for each hazard found, the correct first response — including why water never goes on an oil fire.

themes.theme: Clean as you go
themes.description: The wash-rinse-sanitise order, cloths that spread rather than clean, and leaving a station ready for the next person.
themes.transfer_check: Cook one simple dish and finish with the station inspection-clean, narrating the order you cleaned in and why.

themes.theme: Cold: the fridge as a system
themes.description: Cold chain, shelf order, and why raw meat lives at the bottom.
themes.transfer_check: Audit a real fridge against safe shelf order and temperature, fix what is wrong, and log what you changed.

themes.theme: Measuring, tasting, adjusting
themes.description: Weights beat cups, tasting is a step not a treat, and salt-acid-fat-heat as the levers of adjustment.
themes.transfer_check: Season a bland base (soup or grain) to genuinely good by iterating taste-adjust-taste, recording each move you made.

themes.theme: The recipe as a plan, not a script
themes.description: Reading a recipe once through, mise en place, and knowing which lines are law and which are suggestion.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare full mise en place for a new recipe, then cook it without re-reading, marking beforehand the two lines that must not be improvised.

themes.theme: Tools you do not need
themes.description: What a knife, a pan and a pot replace, and how to judge a gadget before it takes the drawer.
themes.transfer_check: Cook a dish 'as seen' that normally uses a specialised gadget, using only basic tools, and compare results.

themes.theme: A meal from a bare cupboard
themes.description: The pantry backbone — grain, allium, fat, acid, tinned protein — and building dinner when there is 'nothing in'.
themes.transfer_check: Cook a complete meal using only what is already in a real cupboard, listing what you used and what the meal cost.

tracks.name: What food is: nutrition without the noise

themes.theme: Energy, and where it hides
themes.description: Calories as fuel, portion reality versus package fiction, and the drinks that are meals.
themes.transfer_check: Estimate the energy in one of your own typical days, then check against labels and a reference and report where you were most wrong.

themes.theme: Protein, and who needs how much
themes.description: What protein is for, the plant and animal sources, and need across childhood, training, pregnancy and old age.
themes.transfer_check: Plan one real day of meals that meets the protein need of a named person unlike yourself, with sources shown.

themes.theme: Carbohydrates: the fast and the slow
themes.description: Whole versus refined, fibre as the difference, and why the same sugar behaves differently inside an apple and a soda.
themes.transfer_check: Swap one refined staple in your week for a whole version and record the swap's cost, taste and how it held your hunger.

themes.theme: Fats: needed, chosen, hidden
themes.description: Cooking fats, essential fats and the fats that arrive uninvited in packaged food.
themes.transfer_check: Find the fat content and type in five packaged foods you actually eat and rank them against what you assumed.

themes.theme: Reading a label in twenty seconds
themes.description: Per-100g versus per-portion, the ingredient list as a story told in descending order, and the claims on the front that mean nothing.
themes.transfer_check: Given two competing products, pick the better one using only the label, and defend the pick in four sentences.

themes.theme: Vitamins, minerals and the short list that runs low
themes.description: Iron, iodine, B12, vitamin D and calcium — who actually runs short, and the foods that fix it before pills do.
themes.transfer_check: For a named diet (vegan, low-dairy, low-sun), identify the likely gap and plan a week of real foods that closes it.

themes.theme: Water, caffeine and what you drink all day
themes.description: Hydration reality versus myth, caffeine's arc through a day, and the quiet calories in what pours.
themes.transfer_check: Log everything you drink for three days and redesign the pattern with one change you can keep.

themes.theme: Ultra-processed: what the term actually marks
themes.description: The formulation-versus-food distinction, why these products are engineered to be easy to keep eating, and where the evidence stands.
themes.transfer_check: Sort a week of your own shopping into whole, processed and ultra-processed, and name the one swap with the best effort-to-benefit ratio.

themes.theme: Diets, claims and who profits
themes.description: Reading a nutrition claim like a Signal Reader: the study behind the headline, the influencer's sponsor, the before-after photo.
themes.transfer_check: Take one current diet claim from your feed, trace its evidence, and deliver a verdict a friend could act on.

themes.theme: Eating patterns that hold
themes.description: Why patterns beat rules: regular meals, plates built around plants and protein, and change that survives a bad week.
themes.transfer_check: Design one realistic weekly eating pattern for yourself, follow it for a week, and report what held and what needs redesign.

tracks.name: Feeding people: planning, budget and the shop

themes.theme: The week on one page
themes.description: Meal planning that survives reality: anchor meals, flex nights and the leftovers written into the plan.
themes.transfer_check: Write a one-page plan for a real week, cook it, and mark what the plan got wrong for next time.

themes.theme: The list, and the shop that follows it
themes.description: Building a list from the plan, the store's layout as persuasion, and endcaps designed to break your budget.
themes.transfer_check: Do one real shop from a written list, note every deviation and what triggered it, and total the cost of the deviations.

themes.theme: Price per unit, not price per package
themes.description: Unit pricing, brand ladders and when the big pack is actually the expensive one.
themes.transfer_check: In a real aisle, find three cases where the obvious choice loses on unit price, with photos or figures.

themes.theme: Feeding four for less
themes.description: The cheap backbone proteins and grains, stretching meat, and the cuisines that mastered low-cost cooking long ago.
themes.transfer_check: Cook a family-sized meal under a set per-head budget and publish the costed recipe.

themes.theme: Cooking once, eating thrice
themes.description: Batch cooking, the fridge-freezer relay, and containers that make leftovers get eaten instead of feared.
themes.transfer_check: Batch-cook one base and serve it as three genuinely different meals across a week.

themes.theme: Waste: the food you paid for and threw away
themes.description: Date labels decoded (use-by versus best-before), storage that extends life, and the bin audit that changes behaviour.
themes.transfer_check: Audit one week of a real household's discarded food, price it, and change two storage or planning habits in response.

themes.theme: The seasons and the price of distance
themes.description: Why produce has a season and a price curve, and what freezing and tinning preserve of it.
themes.transfer_check: Compare the price and origin of one vegetable across fresh-in-season, fresh-out-of-season, frozen and tinned, and pick a policy for your household.

themes.theme: Feeding people who eat differently
themes.description: Allergy, faith, choice and medical diets at one table — planning one meal that works for everyone without cooking four dinners.
themes.transfer_check: Plan and cook one meal that safely serves a real mixed table (including one allergy or restriction), and explain your cross-contact controls.

themes.theme: When money runs short before the week does
themes.description: Food banks, community meals, benefits that cover food, and cooking through a genuinely empty stretch with dignity.
themes.transfer_check: Map the food support within reach of your own address — eligibility, hours, what to bring — into a half-page guide someone could use tomorrow.

themes.theme: Hosting: the meal as an event
themes.description: Scaling a recipe, the timeline written backwards from sitting down, and the dishes that let the host be at their own table.
themes.transfer_check: Host a real meal for four or more: publish your backwards timeline and serve everything within fifteen minutes of plan.

themes.theme: The invisible passengers
themes.description: Bacteria, viruses and toxins in food — which ones cause most illness, and the four controls (clean, separate, cook, chill) that stop them.
themes.transfer_check: For one real meal you cook, name the hazard most likely present at each step and the control you applied.

themes.theme: Temperature: the danger zone
themes.description: The 5–60°C band, safe internal temperatures by food, and why a thermometer beats every rule of thumb.
themes.transfer_check: Cook a protein to its safe internal temperature verified with a real thermometer, and chart the cooling of the leftovers into safe storage.

themes.theme: Cross-contact and the separate board
themes.description: Raw-to-ready pathways: boards, cloths, hands and the sink itself as the crossing points.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare a raw-meat dish and a salad in one session with demonstrably zero cross-contact, narrating your controls.

themes.theme: Hands, hair and being clean enough to cook
themes.description: When handwashing actually matters, gloves as false comfort, and cooking while ill.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the full handwash at the moments that require it during one cooking session, and name the two moments people skip.

themes.theme: Leftovers: the second life of a meal
themes.description: Cooling fast, reheating hot, the counting of days, and the foods that do not get a second chance (rice included).
themes.transfer_check: Take real leftovers through cool-store-reheat with times and temperatures logged, and bin-or-keep three fridge items with reasons.

themes.theme: Allergens: the eight that matter most
themes.description: The major allergens, reading them off labels and menus, and why 'a little bit' is not safe.
themes.transfer_check: Screen a real packaged meal and a restaurant menu for a named allergen, including the may-contain judgement call.

themes.theme: Preserving: the old technologies
themes.description: Salt, sugar, acid, heat and cold — how jam, pickles and tins actually work, and where home preserving goes dangerous (botulism and the low-acid jar).
themes.transfer_check: Make one safe high-acid preserve with correct process, and explain why the same jar of green beans would need a pressure canner.

themes.theme: Water you can cook with
themes.description: When tap water is the standard, when it is not (advisories, travel, wells), and making water safe.
themes.transfer_check: Find your own water supplier's latest quality report, and demonstrate one field method of making questionable water safe.

themes.theme: When food goes wrong anyway
themes.description: Recognising food poisoning, who is at real risk (pregnant, young, old, immunocompromised), and when it is a clinic call.
themes.transfer_check: Given three illness scenarios, decide home-care versus clinic versus emergency for each, and name the food rule that was likely broken.

themes.theme: Feeding the vulnerable
themes.description: The stricter rules for infants, pregnancy and elders: the foods excluded, the temperatures raised, the dates hardened.
themes.transfer_check: Adapt one family recipe so it is safe for a named vulnerable eater, listing each change and the rule behind it.

tracks.name: Food, culture and the wider system

themes.theme: Where dinner comes from
themes.description: The chain from farm to plate — growing, processing, moving, selling — and the hands it passes through.
themes.transfer_check: Trace one item from your own plate back to its origin as far as evidence allows, documenting each link you can verify.

themes.theme: The dish that carries a people
themes.description: Food as heritage: why dishes migrate with people, and what a recipe preserves that a museum cannot.
themes.transfer_check: Learn one dish from someone of a tradition not your own, cook it to their approval, and record its story as they tell it.

themes.theme: The family recipe as an archive
themes.description: Oral recipes, the pinch and the handful, and writing down what an elder cooks before it is lost.
themes.transfer_check: Document one real family or community recipe from its keeper — quantities, technique and story — into a form a stranger could cook from.

themes.theme: The table as a practice
themes.description: Shared meals and what they measurably do for households, and the hospitality codes different cultures build around food.
themes.transfer_check: Run a device-free shared meal with real people, applying one hospitality practice from a culture you researched, and reflect on what changed.

themes.theme: What food costs the planet
themes.description: Land, water and emissions by food type — the honest hierarchy, and why the biggest lever is usually waste, not the exotic swap.
themes.transfer_check: Rank five of your staple foods by environmental footprint using published data, and make one evidence-based change you can sustain.

themes.theme: The people who grow and serve
themes.description: Farm labour, kitchen labour and delivery labour: the working conditions inside the price of a meal.
themes.transfer_check: Investigate the labour behind one food you buy weekly and present what its price does and does not pay for.

themes.theme: Food deserts and food swamps
themes.description: Why some neighbourhoods have six chicken shops and no greengrocer, and what access actually determines about diet.
themes.transfer_check: Map real food access within walking distance of two different addresses in your area and compare what a week's healthy shop would take at each.

themes.theme: Marketing on a plate
themes.description: How food is sold — to children especially: placement, packaging, cartoon spokesmen and the school-adjacent economy.
themes.transfer_check: Collect five food marketing techniques aimed at children from real shelves or screens and redesign one advert to sell the honest version.

themes.theme: Growing something you eat
themes.description: One pot, one windowsill, one bed: the shortest possible supply chain and what tending it teaches.
themes.transfer_check: Grow one edible plant from start to harvest, log its care, and cook what you grew.

themes.theme: Feeding the future
themes.description: How the food system might feed ten billion — precision agriculture, alternative proteins, redistribution — and how to judge each claim.
themes.transfer_check: Take one 'future of food' claim, examine the strongest evidence for and against, and stake a defensible position in one page.
